hypothesis: The KEGG ortholog K03825 (putative acetyltransferase, EC:2.3.1.-) is increased or characteristic of the gut metagenome of 5-month-old infants relative to 12-month-old infants.
rationale: Multiple targeted searches for the specific KEGG ortholog identifier K03825 (alone, and combined with infant gut microbiome/age/complementary feeding terms) returned only database entries (KEGG KO page, annotation dumps such as ggkbase/KEGGDecoder definition files, and supplementary KO lists) and no primary study reporting this KO as differentially abundant between younger (~5 month, pre/early complementary feeding) and older (~12 month) infants, or in any age/diet contrast. K03825 is an unclassified, poorly characterized 'putative acetyltransferase' (GNAT-family-like) with no assigned KEGG pathway or BRITE category, so it is essentially never singled out in published infant metagenomic analyses, which typically report at pathway/module level. What I did find is only generic, pathway-level context: primary studies do document that the infant gut metagenome's functional repertoire shifts with age and with the transition from milk-based to solid feeding (e.g. increased carbohydrate/plant-polysaccharide utilization and Firmicutes activity by/after ~6 months), while at least one longitudinal complementary-feeding metagenomic+metabolomic study explicitly reported that overall KEGG functional capacity remained comparatively stable across 4, 9 and 12 months even as taxonomy diversified. That literature provides no directional support specific to a putative acetyltransferase KO, and it neither confirms nor refutes enrichment at 5 months. Per the rubric this is 'only generic/pathway-level or theoretical reasoning found (no study on this specific feature+group combination)' with something relevant located, i.e. score 1 rather than 0 (searches were not entirely empty of relevant context) and not -1 (no study reports this KO in the opposite direction).

evidence.title: Adaptation of the infant gut microbiome during the complementary feeding transition
evidence.study_population: Healthy human infants sampled longitudinally at ~4, ~9 and ~12 months of age (shotgun metagenomics with KEGG functional assignment plus LC-MS metabolomics)
evidence.relevance: Closest available design to the 5- vs 12-month contrast with KEGG-level functional profiling; provides pathway-level context but reports that gut microbiome functional capacity stayed relatively stable across the first year while taxonomy diversified, and does not report K03825 or any putative acetyltransferase ortholog as characteristic of the younger timepoint.

evidence.title: Feasibility of Metatranscriptome Analysis from Infant Gut Microbiota: Adaptation to Solid Foods Results in Increased Activity of Firmicutes at Six Months
evidence.study_population: Infant(s) sampled around the introduction of solid foods (~6 months of age), fecal metatranscriptome/metagenome
evidence.relevance: Primary evidence that microbial functional gene expression (e.g. sugar transport, Firmicutes activity) changes around the milk-to-solids transition, establishing that age-related functional shifts occur; however it provides no data on K03825 specifically or on its direction between 5 and 12 months.

evidence.title: Comparative characterization of the infant gut microbiome and their maternal lineage by a multi-omics approach
evidence.study_population: Human infants compared with mothers and grandmothers; ~9,867 KEGG Orthologs quantified from fecal metagenomes
evidence.relevance: Demonstrates that KO-level (KEGG ortholog) differences between age groups are detectable and commonly analyzed at pathway aggregate level; used here only as generic support that KO-level age effects exist, since no result for K03825 in a 5- vs 12-month infant comparison was found.

evidence.title: KEGG ORTHOLOGY: K03825
evidence.relevance: Confirms the identity of the feature as a putative acetyltransferase KO with minimal functional/pathway annotation, explaining why no infant-specific literature on this ortholog exists and why only unclassified-enzyme reasoning is possible.

contradicting_evidence: No study reporting K03825 enriched in older (12-month) versus younger infants was found, so there is no direct contradiction. The only mildly discordant finding is that the longitudinal complementary-feeding metagenomic study (PLOS One 2022) reported overall KEGG functional capacity to be largely stable from ~4 to ~12 months, which weakens (but does not reverse) an expectation of strong age-differential abundance for an individual unclassified acetyltransferase KO.

caveats: K03825 is an 'unclassified' KEGG ortholog with a non-specific EC (2.3.1.-) and no pathway/BRITE assignment; such generic KOs are rarely reported individually in publications, so absence of literature reflects reporting conventions and annotation ambiguity as much as biology. Homologous GNAT-family acetyltransferases are widespread across bacterial genomes, meaning abundance of this KO may largely track taxonomic composition (e.g. Bifidobacterium/Enterobacteriaceae dominance at 5 months vs Firmicutes expansion at 12 months) rather than a discrete metabolic function; interpretation should therefore be taxonomy-aware. Searches were limited to English-language web-indexed sources and supplementary KO tables in published papers are often not text-indexed, so a relevant supplementary-level report could have been missed.
